newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate leader wants to read Lake's FBI file.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate leader wants to read Lake's FBI file.

text.p: Saying there were three areas of concern about the nomination of Anthony Lake to head the CIA, Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said on Sunday he had offered to screen Lake's FBI file.
"It's at least three very critical areas," he told the CBS programme "Face the Nation."

Lott said that Intelligence Committee Chairman Richard Shelby "has said: 'Look, this is going to be fair and nonpartisan, but it is very important. Here's an agency that's been under attack, that's had major proglems.'"
"We better make sure we have a new director that is as clean as possible and has a reputation, and in fact absolutely is a man of integrity and veracity," Lott said.

"So when there's an indication that maybe he misled or even did not tell the truth ... to a House committee on some of his actions in his previous position," Lott said. "That is a major concern. That goes to basic integrity."
The White House has not replied to his offer to screen the FBI file, which has been requested -- rather than a summary -- by 10 members of the Senate.
"If I do that, and I find a real concern, they (the Clinton administration) are going to have to free up this information," Lott said.

He said the file should also be examined by the chairman and ranking members of the Intelligence Committee. If problems were discovered, Lott said, the White House would have two choices: "either withdraw the nomination or make the file available for senators to review."

"This is not secretary of the interior or secretary of commerce. This is the head of the Central Intelligence Agency, a very critical agency," he said. "And to make sure that this person is clean and doesn't have any problems in his background, I think we have to go the extra mile, to make sure we know what is in his background, including what is in his FBI file."
When asked if Lake's nomination was in trouble, Lott replied: "It could be." However, he said he had not advised the White House to pull the nomination.
Lott said he had seen a published report that "Tony Lake was looking at what he was prepared to have released as part of the nomination process."

"That's not his choice," Lott told CBS. "We need to have everything in his background. I saw last week where he suggested that maybe he didn't want to put some of lhis stock ownership in trust, even though the companies might have some dealings with the CIA. That's totally unacceptable."
Chairman Jesse Helms of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee moved last week to defeat Lake's nomination.

Helms, the North Carolina Republican who is the sole member of the Senate to announce his opposition publicly, cited what he called a "clear pattern of contempt and disregard" for Congress by Lake, President Clinton's first-term national security adviser.
In a letter to Shelby, Helms accused Lake of having engaged in "political gamesmanship" with U.S. national security interests.

He cited Lake's decision to keep Congress in the dark about the administration's tacit approval of Iranian arms shipments to Bosnian Moslems in 1994 in breach of a U.N. weapons embargo publicly backed by Washington.

Helms also cited what he called Lake's refusal to advise Clinton to levy sanctions on China for its alleged missile sales to Iran, and his "cavalier dismissal" of Senate requests for information on a proposed chemical weapons convention.
Lake's twice-postponed confirmation hearings were scheduled to begin on March 11 before the intelligence committee.
